## The Netflix rating-prediction pipeline {.detail-slide .netflix-workflow-slide}

<div class="netflix-example-input" role="img" aria-label="One observed Netflix training triple and one Netflix test pair whose rating is hidden during prediction">
<div class="netflix-train-example"><span>TRAIN.CSV: OBSERVED TRIPLE</span><b>(1960, 670, 4)</b><p>User 1960 gave movie 670 four stars. The model may learn from this row.</p></div>
<div class="netflix-test-example"><span>TEST.CSV: PREDICTION PAIR</span><b>(1574, 2956, ?)</b><p>The model sees the user and movie. The rating stays hidden until evaluation.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="lesson-path five-stage-path netflix-five-stage" role="img" aria-label="The Netflix example moves from data inspection and preprocessing through baseline modeling, evaluation, and ranking">
<div><span>01</span><b>Inspect</b><p><code>train</code> has 51,161 observed triples with user, movie and rating.</p></div>
<i>then</i>
<div class="preprocess-stage"><span>02</span><b>Standardize IDs</b><p>Fit shared ID maps. Create <code>X_train</code>, <code>y_train</code> and <code>X_test</code>.</p></div>
<i>then</i>
<div><span>03</span><b>Fit a predictor</b><p>Learn an abstract scoring rule <code>f_theta</code> from the training arrays.</p></div>
<i>then</i>
<div><span>04</span><b>Predict and evaluate</b><p>Compute <code>y_pred</code>. Reveal <code>y_test</code> only when calculating RMSE.</p></div>
<i>then</i>
<div><span>05</span><b>Rank</b><p>For user 1960, movies 2098, 898 and 2195 are ordered by <code>y_pred</code>.</p></div>
</div>

<p class="baseline-takeaway netflix-workflow-takeaway"><b>Row alignment stays fixed:</b> <code>X_test[j]</code> receives <code>y_pred[j]</code>, which is later compared with <code>y_test[j]</code>.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- The train and test sizes come from the course files in `dataset/netflix/` in the public STAT3009 repository.
- The displayed training triple and test pair are the first rows of the public course `train.csv` and `test.csv` files. The test rating is shown as hidden because prediction code must not read it.
- The predictor remains abstract here so that data preparation and the prediction contract appear before any specific baseline method.
:::

## A baseline must score every test pair {.detail-slide .baseline-contract-slide}

<div class="baseline-contract compact-contract" role="img" aria-label="Training ratings produce a baseline model, which predicts each test pair and receives an RMSE score">
<div><span>TRAINING RATINGS</span><b>Ω<sup>tr</sup></b><p>Information the model may use.</p></div>
<i>fit</i>
<div><span>PREDICTION RULE</span><b>f(u, i)</b><p>A complete rule, including fallbacks.</p></div>
<i>predict</i>
<div><span>TEST PAIRS</span><b>(u, i)</b><p>Pairs excluded from model fitting.</p></div>
<i>score</i>
<div><span>TEST RMSE</span><b>lower is better</b><p>One comparable number for every method.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="baseline-requirements">
<p><b>Simple</b><span>We can explain every prediction.</span></p>
<p><b>Complete</b><span>New users and movies still receive a score.</span></p>
<p><b>Reproducible</b><span>The same training data gives the same benchmark.</span></p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- The prediction and held-out evaluation contract follows the setup introduced in the overview lecture and the course notebook.
:::

## Data preprocessing: categorical IDs {.detail-slide .id-encoding-concept-slide}

<p class="encoding-intro"><b>User and item IDs are labels.</b> The model needs stable array indices, but the spelling or numerical size of an ID carries no preference information.</p>

<div class="encoding-demo encoding-demo-animated" role="img" aria-label="Separate user and movie label encoders map repeated string identifiers to consecutive integer indices">
<div class="encoding-track">
<span>USER LABELS</span>
<code>[&quot;U_A&quot;, &quot;U_Z&quot;, &quot;U_A&quot;]</code>
<i class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">fit user vocabulary</i>
<span class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">USER INDICES</span>
<code class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">[0, 1, 0]</code>
</div>
<div class="encoding-track movie-track">
<span>MOVIE LABELS</span>
<code>[&quot;M_B&quot;, &quot;M_A&quot;, &quot;M_C&quot;]</code>
<i class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1">fit movie vocabulary</i>
<span class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1">MOVIE INDICES</span>
<code class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1">[1, 0, 2]</code>
</div>
</div>

<div class="id-index-explanation fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2">
<div><span>RAW LABEL</span><b><code>"U_Z"</code></b><p>An identifier. Its characters carry no distance or order.</p></div>
<i></i>
<div><span>ARRAY INDEX</span><b><code>1</code></b><p>A valid zero-based position in a NumPy array.</p></div>
</div>

<p class="baseline-takeaway fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3"><b>Use two encoders:</b> users and movies have separate vocabularies, even when both happen to be integers.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- `LabelEncoder` maps a one-dimensional set of labels to integer values from zero to `n_classes - 1`: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.LabelEncoder.html.
- The string IDs are illustrative. The course files already use compact numerical IDs, but the generic preprocessing interface should also work with arbitrary labels.
- Animation sequence: encode user labels, encode movie labels, interpret the resulting index, then state the separate-vocabulary rule.
:::

## sklearn.preprocessing.LabelEncoder {.detail-slide .label-encoder-api-slide .code-slide}

<div class="le-api-import fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">
<div><span>PACKAGE</span><b>sklearn</b></div>
<i>.</i>
<div><span>MODULE</span><b>preprocessing</b></div>
<i>.</i>
<div><span>CLASS</span><b>LabelEncoder</b></div>
<code>from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder</code>
</div>

:::: {.columns .le-api-columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```python
enc = LabelEncoder()
labels = ["U_A", "U_Z", "U_A"]

enc.fit(labels)
enc.classes_                       # ["U_A", "U_Z"]

enc.transform(["U_Z", "U_A"])    # [1, 0]
enc.inverse_transform([0, 1])      # ["U_A", "U_Z"]
```
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
<div class="le-api-steps">
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1"><span>01</span><b><code>LabelEncoder()</code></b><em>Creates an encoder with no learned vocabulary.</em></p>
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2"><span>02</span><b><code>fit(labels)</code></b><em>Finds the unique labels and stores them in <code>classes_</code>.</em></p>
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3"><span>03</span><b><code>transform(labels)</code></b><em>Applies the stored mapping to known labels.</em></p>
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="4"><span>04</span><b><code>inverse_transform(indices)</code></b><em>Converts integer indices back to the original labels.</em></p>
</div>
:::
::::

<p class="baseline-takeaway le-api-takeaway fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="5"><code>fit</code> changes the encoder's state. <code>transform</code> reuses that state and cannot invent an index for an unseen label.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Class API and attributes: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.LabelEncoder.html.
- Scikit-learn documents `LabelEncoder` primarily for one-dimensional target labels. In this lecture, separate instances act as simple vocabulary mappers for the one-dimensional user and movie ID columns.
- `classes_` contains the label for each encoded index. `transform` accepts labels from this fitted set, and `inverse_transform` maps indices back to labels.
- Animation sequence: locate the class in the package, create an object, fit its vocabulary, transform labels, invert the mapping, then state the unseen-label limitation.
:::

<div class="le-failure-flow" role="img" aria-label="Animation showing that label encoders fitted only on training IDs cannot transform users and movies that appear only in the test pairs">
<div class="le-data-block le-train-block fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">
<span>TRAIN TRIPLES</span>
<b>Observed ratings</b>
<table><thead><tr><th>user</th><th>movie</th><th>rating</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>U_A</td><td>M_A</td><td>4</td></tr><tr><td>U_C</td><td>M_B</td><td>5</td></tr><tr><td>U_A</td><td>M_B</td><td>3</td></tr></tbody></table>
</div>
<div class="le-flow-arrow le-failure-a1 fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1"><span>fit</span><i></i></div>
<div class="le-train-vocab fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1">

<b>User vocabulary</b>
<code>U_A: 0&nbsp;&nbsp; U_C: 1</code>
<b>Movie vocabulary</b>
<code>M_A: 0&nbsp;&nbsp; M_B: 1</code>
</div>
<div class="le-flow-arrow le-failure-a2 fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2"><span>transform test</span><i></i></div>
<div class="le-data-block le-test-block fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">
<span>TEST PAIRS</span>
<b>Pairs to score</b>
<table><thead><tr><th>user</th><th>movie</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>U_B <strong class="le-unseen-id fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2">unseen</strong></td><td>M_A</td></tr><tr><td>U_C</td><td>M_C <strong class="le-unseen-id fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2">unseen</strong></td></tr></tbody></table>
</div>
</div>

<div class="le-failure-result fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2">
<span>TRANSFORM CANNOT CONTINUE</span>
<code>U_B is absent from the user vocabulary</code>
<code>M_C is absent from the movie vocabulary</code>
</div>

<p class="baseline-takeaway fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3">The course split contains test-only IDs. A train-only encoder cannot assign every scheduled test pair an index.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- The labels in the animation are illustrative.
- In the course split, 74 users and 584 movies occur only in test. The counts come from the public course train/test files.
- A `LabelEncoder` raises an error when `transform` receives a label outside its fitted classes.
- Animation sequence: show the two splits, fit train-only vocabularies, expose the unseen test labels, then state the consequence.
:::

## Shared train–test ID vocabulary {.detail-slide .label-encoder-shared-slide}

<div class="le-shared-flow" role="img" aria-label="Animation showing that train and test ID columns are combined to fit shared user and movie vocabularies, after which each split is transformed separately">
<div class="le-shared-input fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">
<span>ID COLUMNS ONLY</span>
<div><b>train users</b><code>U_A, U_C, U_A</code></div>
<div><b>test users</b><code>U_B, U_C</code></div>
<div><b>train movies</b><code>M_A, M_B, M_B</code></div>
<div><b>test movies</b><code>M_A, M_C</code></div>
</div>
<div class="le-flow-arrow le-shared-a1 fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1"><span>concatenate IDs</span><i></i></div>
<div class="le-shared-vocab fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1">
<span>FIT ONCE</span>
<b>Shared user map</b>
<code>U_A: 0&nbsp;&nbsp; U_B: 1&nbsp;&nbsp; U_C: 2</code>
<b>Shared movie map</b>
<code>M_A: 0&nbsp;&nbsp; M_B: 1&nbsp;&nbsp; M_C: 2</code>
</div>
<div class="le-flow-arrow le-shared-a2 fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2"><span>transform separately</span><i></i></div>
<div class="le-shared-output fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2">
<span>KEEP THE SPLITS</span>
<div><b>encoded train</b><code>[0,0] [2,1] [0,1]</code></div>
<div><b>encoded test</b><code>[1,0] [2,2]</code></div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="le-no-leakage fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3">
<span>WHAT ENTERS THE ENCODER?</span>
<b><code>user_id</code> and <code>movie_id</code></b>
<i></i>
<span>WHAT STAYS OUT?</span>
<b><code>test.rating</code></b>
</div>

<p class="baseline-takeaway fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="4">Concatenation defines a common vocabulary. It does not merge the ratings or move test rows into the training set.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- The example uses the same illustrative labels as the preceding slide.
- This workflow fits vocabularies from the identifiers in a fixed competition-style test set. It does not use held-out ratings.
- In a live system, IDs that arrive after fitting still require an unknown-index policy or a prediction fallback.
- Animation sequence: show the four ID columns, fit shared maps, transform each split separately, then isolate the rating column from the encoder.
:::

## LabelEncoder implementation {.detail-slide .label-encoder-code-slide .code-slide}

:::: {.columns .le-code-columns}
::: {.column width="66%"}
```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

all_users = pd.concat([train["user_id"], test["user_id"]])
all_items = pd.concat([train["movie_id"], test["movie_id"]])

user_enc = LabelEncoder().fit(all_users)
item_enc = LabelEncoder().fit(all_items)

train["u"] = user_enc.transform(train["user_id"])
test["u"]  = user_enc.transform(test["user_id"])
train["i"] = item_enc.transform(train["movie_id"])
test["i"]  = item_enc.transform(test["movie_id"])

n_users = len(user_enc.classes_)
n_items = len(item_enc.classes_)
```
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
<div class="le-code-reading">
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0"><span>01</span><b>Collect ID columns</b><em>No ratings enter <code>all_users</code> or <code>all_items</code>.</em></p>
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1"><span>02</span><b>Fit once</b><em>Each encoder stores one shared vocabulary.</em></p>
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2"><span>03</span><b>Transform separately</b><em>Train and test remain different datasets.</em></p>
</div>
:::
::::

<p class="baseline-takeaway le-code-takeaway fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3"><code>fit</code> defines the mapping. <code>transform</code> applies the same mapping wherever that entity appears.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- API behavior: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.LabelEncoder.html.
- Separate encoders define unrelated user and movie vocabularies.
- The course train/test files already contain compact numerical IDs. This code documents the general preprocessing contract and supports arbitrary string or sparse integer identifiers.
:::

## Data preprocessing: NumPy arrays {.detail-slide .array-contract-slide .code-slide}

<div class="array-contract-flow" role="img" aria-label="Training and test DataFrames are converted into NumPy input matrices and rating vectors; the model predicts a vector aligned with y test">
<div class="array-source train-array-source"><span>TRAIN DATAFRAME</span><b>u, i, rating</b><p>51,161 observed triples</p></div>
<div class="array-split"><i></i><span>split columns</span><i></i></div>
<div class="array-pair">
<p><span>MODEL INPUT</span><b>X_train</b><code>(51161, 2)</code><em>columns [u, i]</em></p>
<p><span>TRAINING TARGET</span><b>y_train</b><code>(51161,)</code><em>observed ratings</em></p>
</div>
<div class="array-model"><span>NUMPY METHOD</span><b>fit on train</b><i></i><b>predict X_test</b></div>
<div class="array-pair test-array-pair">
<p><span>MODEL INPUT</span><b>X_test</b><code>(51161, 2)</code><em>columns [u, i]</em></p>
<p><span>MODEL OUTPUT</span><b>y_pred</b><code>(51161,)</code><em>one score per row</em></p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="array-contract-bottom">
<pre><code>X_train = train[["u", "i"]].to_numpy(dtype=np.int64)
y_train = train["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

X_test = test[["u", "i"]].to_numpy(dtype=np.int64)
y_test = test["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)  # evaluation only</code></pre>

<div class="numpy-method-rule">
<span>IMPLEMENTATION RULE</span>
<b>Pandas prepares the tables.</b>
<b>NumPy fits every baseline and produces <code>y_pred</code>.</b>
<p>During prediction, the method receives <code>X_test</code>. We reveal <code>y_test</code> only when calculating RMSE.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Array shapes follow the public course train/test files, each with 51,161 rows.
- The diagram defines the data interface used by every method in the remainder of this lecture.
- `y_test` is created for classroom evaluation but remains outside every fitting and prediction calculation.
:::

## Leakage-free evaluation {.detail-slide .leakage-slide}

<div class="leakage-flow" role="img" aria-label="Training ratings are used to fit summaries, test pairs receive predictions, and test ratings are used only to calculate RMSE">
<div><span>TRAIN RATINGS</span><b>Fit summaries</b><p>global mean, user effects, movie effects</p></div>
<i>use fitted values</i>
<div><span>TEST IDs</span><b>Generate predictions</b><p>one score for every test row</p></div>
<i>after prediction</i>
<div><span>TEST RATINGS</span><b>Calculate RMSE</b><p>compare truth with predictions</p></div>
</div>

<div class="leakage-warning">
<span>DATA LEAKAGE</span>
<b>Computing a user or movie mean from <code>pd.concat([train, test])</code> lets test ratings influence the prediction.</b>
<p>Use both files only to describe the dataset universe, never to fit a predictive quantity.</p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- The separation follows the train/test contract in the course notebook.
- The leakage example is instructor-authored for this lecture.
:::

## RMSE as the common scoreboard {.detail-slide .metric-protocol-slide}

:::: {.columns .vcenter}
::: {.column width="48%"}
<div class="rmse-formula-large compact-rmse-formula">
$$
\operatorname{RMSE}
=
\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\mathrm{test}}}(y_j-\hat y_j)^2}
$$
</div>

<p class="metric-reading"><b>Interpretation</b><span>Typical prediction error, expressed on the 1–5 rating scale, with larger misses penalized more heavily.</span></p>
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```python
def rmse(y_true, y_pred):
    error = np.asarray(y_true) - np.asarray(y_pred)
    return np.sqrt(np.mean(error ** 2))

# test ratings enter only here
score = rmse(y_test, y_pred)
```

<div class="metric-contract"><span>EVERY METHOD RETURNS</span><b>51,161 predictions</b><p>in the same row order as <code>test</code></p></div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- RMSE and the function signature follow cells 26 and 31–32 of the course notebook.
- This is a compact recall of the metric introduced in the overview lecture.
:::

## From training triples to a prediction vector {.detail-slide .prediction-vector-slide}

<div class="prediction-vector-flow" role="img" aria-label="Training triples determine a prediction rule, then each test user movie pair receives one prediction in a row-aligned rating vector">
<div class="train-triples-stage">
<span class="pipeline-label">TRAIN · THREE-COLUMN LIST OF (u, i, r)</span>
<table aria-label="Example training user movie rating triples">
<thead><tr><th>u</th><th>i</th><th>r</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>

<tr><td>686</td><td>3032</td><td>5</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</div>

<div class="pipeline-connector fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0"><span>summarize</span><i></i></div>

<div class="fitted-rule-stage fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1">
<span class="pipeline-label">PREDICTION RULE</span>
<b>r̂<sub>ui</sub> = rule(u, i)</b>
<p>Use quantities calculated only from <code>train</code>.</p>
<div class="model-patterns"><span>global level</span><span>user pattern</span><span>movie pattern</span></div>
</div>

<div class="pipeline-connector fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2"><span>apply row by row</span><i></i></div>

<div class="test-vector-stage fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3">

</ol>

## Global mean baseline {.formula-slide .real-result-slide}

<div class="formula-stage">
<span>ONE NUMBER FROM TRAIN</span>
$$
\mu=\frac{1}{|\Omega^{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{(u,i)\in\Omega^{\mathrm{tr}}}r_{ui}
\qquad
\hat r_{ui}=\mu
$$
</div>

<div class="real-result-strip">
<p><span>TRAINING MEAN</span><b>3.621</b></p>
<p><span>TEST RMSE</span><b>1.085</b></p>
<p><span>UNSEEN IDS</span><b>Always defined</b></p>
</div>

<p class="baseline-takeaway">The rating distribution gives us a stronger constant prediction than an arbitrary midpoint such as three stars.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Values were calculated from the STAT3009 course train/test files using the displayed formula.
:::

## User mean baseline {.formula-slide .real-result-slide}

<div class="formula-stage user-formula">
<span>ONE NUMBER PER OBSERVED USER</span>
$$
\bar r_u=\frac{1}{|\mathcal I_u^{\mathrm{tr}}|}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_u^{\mathrm{tr}}}r_{ui}
$$
</div>

<div class="baseline-rule-row">
<p><span>KNOWN USER</span><b>r̂<sub>ui</sub> = r̄<sub>u</sub></b><em>same prediction for every movie</em></p>
<p><span>NEW USER</span><b>r̂<sub>ui</sub> = μ</b><em>fall back to the global mean</em></p>
</div>

<div class="real-result-strip two-result-strip">
<p><span>TEST RMSE</span><b>1.017</b></p>
<p><span>CHANGE FROM GLOBAL</span><b>−0.069</b></p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

- Test result uses a global-mean fallback for the 74 test users unseen in training.

## User mean in NumPy {.detail-slide .numpy-group-helper-slide .code-slide}

:::: {.columns .vcenter .numpy-helper-columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
```python
user_mean = np.full(n_users, global_mean)

for u in np.unique(X_train[:, 0]):
    user_mean[u] = np.mean(y_train[X_train[:, 0] == u])

y_pred_user = user_mean[X_test[:, 0]]
```
:::

::: {.column width="39%"}
<div class="user-mask-example">
<span>EXAMPLE · USER u = 1</span>
<p><b>User column</b><code>[0, 1, 0, 2, 1]</code></p>
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0"><b>Boolean mask</b><code>[F, T, F, F, T]</code></p>
<p class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1"><b>Selected ratings</b><code>[1, 2]</code></p>
<div class="user-mask-result fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2">
<b>user_mean[1]</b><code>1.5</code>
</div>
</div>
:::
::::

<div class="group-helper-reading">
<p><b>Build the lookup vector from train</b><span><code>X_train[:, 0] == u</code> selects the ratings from user <code>u</code>.</span></p>
<p><b>Predict by array indexing</b><span>Each encoded test user retrieves one value from <code>user_mean</code>.</span></p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- `user_mean` is a NumPy lookup vector indexed by the encoded user ID.
- The loop visits only user IDs observed in training. Users seen only in the test set retain the pre-filled global mean.
- The final line creates one prediction for every row of `X_test` without another Python loop.
- Animation sequence: show one encoded user column, reveal the Boolean mask, reveal the selected ratings, and then their mean.
:::

## Item mean baseline {.formula-slide .real-result-slide}

<div class="formula-stage item-formula">
<span>ONE NUMBER PER OBSERVED MOVIE</span>
$$
\bar r_i=\frac{1}{|\mathcal U_i^{\mathrm{tr}}|}
\sum_{u\in\mathcal U_i^{\mathrm{tr}}}r_{ui}
$$
</div>

<div class="baseline-rule-row">
<p><span>KNOWN MOVIE</span><b>r̂<sub>ui</sub> = r̄<sub>i</sub></b><em>same prediction for every user</em></p>
<p><span>NEW MOVIE</span><b>r̂<sub>ui</sub> = μ</b><em>fall back to the global mean</em></p>
</div>

<div class="real-result-strip two-result-strip">
<p><span>TEST RMSE</span><b>1.052</b></p>
<p><span>CHANGE FROM GLOBAL</span><b>−0.034</b></p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- Formula follows the item-average method in the original course deck.
- Test result uses a global-mean fallback for the 584 test movies unseen in training.
:::

## Three-mean baseline {.section-break .additive-section}

<div class="section-number">03</div>
<img class="section-crest" src="../Lec-overview-quarto/figs/cu_logo.webp" alt="CUHK emblem">
<p>Take the arithmetic average of the user mean, item mean, and global mean.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- This section uses an instructor-selected equal-weight combination of three previously calculated means.
:::

## Arithmetic average of three means {.additive-intuition-slide}

<div class="additive-equation additive-equation-revised">
<div class="additive-kicker">THREE NUMBERS · EQUAL WEIGHT</div>
<div class="additive-term">user mean</div>
<div class="additive-plus">+</div>
<div class="additive-term">item mean</div>
<div class="additive-plus">+</div>
<div class="additive-term">global mean</div>
</div>

<div class="additive-interpretation">
<p><span>r̄<sub>u</sub></span><b>User mean</b><em>User u's average training rating.</em></p>
<p><span>r̄<sub>i</sub></span><b>Item mean</b><em>Movie i's average training rating.</em></p>
<p><span>μ</span><b>Global mean</b><em>The average over every training rating.</em></p>
</div>

<div class="additive-main-formula compact-additive-formula">
$$\hat r_{ui}=\frac{\bar r_u+\bar r_i+\mu}{3}$$
</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- The formula assigns equal weight to the user, item, and global means.
:::

## Flexible weights {.detail-slide .flex-weight-slide}

<div class="flex-weight-formula">
$$
\hat r_{ui}
=
w_u\bar r_u+w_i\bar r_i+w_0\mu,
\qquad
w_u+w_i+w_0=1
$$
</div>

<div class="flex-weight-reading">
<p><span>USER WEIGHT</span><b>w<sub>u</sub></b><em>Controls how much the user's rating tendency contributes.</em></p>
<p><span>ITEM WEIGHT</span><b>w<sub>i</sub></b><em>Controls how much the movie's average rating contributes.</em></p>
<p><span>GLOBAL WEIGHT</span><b>w<sub>0</sub></b><em>Pulls the prediction toward the overall rating level.</em></p>
</div>

<div class="flex-weight-choice">
<span>CHOICE USED TODAY</span>
<b>w<sub>u</sub> = w<sub>i</sub> = w<sub>0</sub> = 1/3</b>
<p>Equal weights give a simple average. Other weights give different averages without changing the prediction workflow.</p>
</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- This slide presents the general weighted-average form as a conceptual extension.
- All calculations in this lecture continue to use one-third for each mean.
:::

<div class="three-number-example" role="img" aria-label="For user 1960 and movie 2098, average the user mean, item mean, and global mean to obtain the predicted rating">
<div class="three-number-term"><span>USER 1960 MEAN</span><b>3.816</b></div>
<i class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0">+</i>
<div class="three-number-term fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="0"><span>MOVIE 2098 MEAN</span><b>4.000</b></div>
<i class="fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1">+</i>
<div class="three-number-term fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="1"><span>GLOBAL MEAN</span><b>3.621</b></div>
<div class="three-number-divide fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2"><span>DIVIDE THE SUM BY</span><b>3</b></div>
<i class="three-number-equals fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="2">=</i>

</div>

<p class="three-mean-fallback fragment fade-in" data-fragment-index="3"><b>Missing user or item mean</b><span>Put the global mean into the missing slot, then average the same three positions.</span></p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- User 1960's training mean is 3.8155619596541785 and movie 2098's training mean is 4.0.
- Their equal-weight three-mean prediction is `(3.8155619596541785 + 4.0 + 3.621156740485917) / 3 = 3.8122395667133655`.
:::

## Three-mean baseline in Python {.review-slide .code-slide .three-mean-code-slide}

:::: {.columns .vcenter}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```python
u_test = X_test[:, 0]
i_test = X_test[:, 1]

# The mean arrays already contain the global fallback
user_term = user_mean[u_test]
item_term = item_mean[i_test]

y_pred_three = (user_term + item_term + global_mean) / 3

round(rmse(y_test, y_pred_three), 3)
```
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
<div class="console-result additive-console-result">
<span>OUTPUT</span>
<b>1.005</b>
</div>

<div class="code-reading">
<p><b>Equal weights</b><span>each mean contributes one third</span></p>
<p><b>Missing group mean</b><span>replace it with the global mean</span></p>
<p><b>Complete output</b><span>every test row receives a score</span></p>
</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- NumPy code implements the equal-weight average of user, item, and global means on the public course files.
- Output was independently verified from those files.
:::

<div class="ranking-user"><span>EXAMPLE TEST USER</span><b>User 1960</b><p>347 training ratings · training mean 3.82</p></div>

<table class="baseline-table ranking-example-table">
<thead><tr><th>Candidate movie</th><th>Global</th><th>User mean</th><th>Item mean</th><th>Three-mean</th><th>Observed test rating</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Movie 2098</td><td>3.62</td><td>3.82</td><td>4.00</td><td><b>3.81</b></td><td>4</td></tr>
<tr><td>Movie 898</td><td>3.62</td><td>3.82</td><td>3.75</td><td><b>3.73</b></td><td>4</td></tr>
<tr><td>Movie 2195</td><td>3.62</td><td>3.82</td><td>2.40</td><td><b>3.28</b></td><td>2</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<div class="ranking-observation">
<p><b>Global and user means produce ties</b><span>They cannot order movies for one user.</span></p>
<p><b>Three-mean scores vary by movie</b><span>Sorting the three-mean column gives 2098, 898, 2195.</span></p>
</div>

<p class="baseline-takeaway">For one user, the user and global terms are constant. The three-mean score therefore preserves the item-mean order while pulling scores toward the center.</p>

## What the three-mean model cannot explain {.detail-slide .interaction-gap-slide}

<div class="interaction-equation">
<div><span>THREE-MEAN MODEL</span><b>(μ + r̄<sub>u</sub> + r̄<sub>i</sub>) / 3</b><p>Separate average tendencies with equal weights.</p></div>
<i>leaves</i>
<div><span>UNEXPLAINED ERROR</span><b>r<sub>ui</sub> − r̂<sub>ui</sub></b><p>Preference specific to this user–movie pairing.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="interaction-example">
<p><b>A strict rater can still love one movie.</b><span>The user's low average pulls every prediction down, but it cannot represent a special match.</span></p>
<p><b>A popular movie can still be wrong for one user.</b><span>The movie's high average pulls every prediction up, but it cannot represent individual incompatibility.</span></p>
</div>

<p class="baseline-takeaway">Collaborative filtering models the user–movie interaction that separate averages cannot represent.</p>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]
- The limitation follows from using separate user and movie average summaries without a user–movie interaction term.
- The examples are conceptual and do not identify specific Netflix customers or movies.
:::
